main.work: Studies in Greek Scenery, Legend and History
main.author: James George Frazer
main.locator: Frazer's discussion of Pausanias and Mount Sipylus; local text, normalized characters 21213-21905
main.excerpt: This is nearly a direct affirmation that the region about Mount Sipylus in Lydia was his native land. The same thing appears, though less directly, from the minute acquaintance he displays with the district and from the evident fondness with which he recurs again and again to its scenery and legends. He had seen the white eagles wheeling above the lonely tarn of Tantalus in the heart of the hills; he had beheld the stately tomb of the same hero on Mount Sipylus, the ruined city at the bottom of the clear lake, the rock-hewn throne of Pelops crowning the dizzy peak that overhangs the cañon, and the dripping rock which popular fancy took for the bereaved Niobe weeping for her children.

narrativeBlocks.title: The scene
narrativeBlocks.body: Frazer discusses Pausanias’ familiarity with Mount Sipylus, including monuments linked with Tantalus, Pelops, and Niobe. Here Frazer is describing an ancient writer’s observations; the paragraph is not Frazer’s own eyewitness confirmation of those heroes.

narrativeBlocks.title: Why it matters
narrativeBlocks.body: Interpretation: places can preserve stories without proving their events. Frazer’s dated scholarship must be checked against the ancient testimony he discusses.

narrativeBlocks.title: Read it carefully
narrativeBlocks.body: Identify each layer of testimony: a legendary association, Pausanias’ description, and Frazer’s discussion of it. None should be silently promoted into direct proof that a legendary event occurred.

narrativeBlocks.title: Carry it forward
narrativeBlocks.body: Landscape gives heroic afterlife a physical address.
